title: The Flood Comes and the LORD Shuts the Door
summary: God tells Noah to enter the ark with his family and with animals, seven pairs of every clean kind and one pair of every unclean kind, and warns that rain will begin in seven days. In Noah's six hundredth year the fountains of the deep burst open and the floodgates of the heavens pour for forty days. The LORD shuts Noah in, the waters rise above the highest mountains, and every living thing on land dies. Only Noah and those with him in the ark remain, while the waters prevail for 150 days.
story: In chapter 6 God announced the flood and gave Noah instructions for the ark, and Noah obeyed. Now the waiting is over. The chapter narrates the judgment itself, and it reads as creation running backward. In Genesis 1, God separated the waters above from the waters below and gathered the seas so dry land could appear. Here those boundaries give way, and the world returns to something like the watery deep of 1:2. Yet in the middle of the undoing, God keeps a small world alive inside the ark. Everything depends on that remnant, because it is through Noah that the promise of the woman's seed must continue.
historical:
The chapter gives a date unlike anything earlier in Genesis: the six hundredth year of Noah's life, the second month, the seventeenth day. The flood narrative in chapters 7 and 8 tracks days and months like a ship's log, and the dates show the waters rising and falling across about a year. Ancient readers had no universal calendar, so events were dated by the years of a ruler or, here, of the one man at the center of the story.

The extent and date of the flood have long been debated (see the hard question below). Excavations in Mesopotamia have turned up thick layers of flood silt at cities such as Ur, Kish, and Shuruppak. In 1929 the archaeologist Leonard Woolley announced that the layer he found at Ur was evidence of the biblical flood. Later work showed that these layers come from different periods and reflect local river floods, which were a real and terrible danger in the flat plain between the Tigris and the Euphrates. Such floods may lie behind the region's flood traditions, but no single deposit can be tied to the flood of Genesis.
cultural:
Israel's later law divided animals into clean and unclean, the clean being those fit for sacrifice and for food (Leviticus 11). Genesis assumes that Noah already knows the difference. The seven pairs of clean animals provide for the sacrifice Noah will offer when he leaves the ark (8:20) and for the diet God will allow after the flood (9:3). The Hebrew phrase is literally seven seven, which can mean seven pairs or seven animals in all; translations differ.

The ancient picture of the world helps explain the chapter's language. Many ancient peoples imagined a solid dome or expanse above the earth holding back waters above it, and a great deep of waters beneath the earth that fed springs and seas. When the text says the fountains of the great deep burst forth and the floodgates (literally windows) of the heavens were opened, it describes both reservoirs released at once. Whatever one concludes about the physical event, the language tells the reader what it means: the order God set in place on the second and third days of creation has been undone.
literary: The chapter moves in slow, repetitive waves that imitate the rising water. Key phrases recur: the ark, the waters, male and female, two by two, as God had commanded, every living thing. The verbs build in intensity. The waters rose, then rose greatly, then rose very greatly, then covered the mountains. Verses 21 to 23 list the dying creatures twice in the language of Genesis 1, and the second list (man, livestock, crawling creatures, birds) runs in the reverse order of their creation, as if the world is being uncreated. Two small sentences stand out against this flood of repetition. “Then the LORD shut him in” (verse 16) is the only thing God is said to do in the chapter beyond speaking, and “only Noah and those with him in the ark remained” (verse 23) is its quiet climax. Many scholars have noticed that the whole flood story from 6:9 to 9:19 is arranged as a mirror, with numbers of days rising to the turning point in 8:1, God remembered Noah, and then falling away. The numbers in this chapter (seven days, forty days, 150 days) are the ascending side of that pattern.

outline.t: Go into the ark: clean and unclean animals
Noah, his family, and the animals enter
The deep and the heavens open; the LORD shuts the door
The waters rise above the mountains
All life on land perishes; only the ark remains

doctrines.note: The flood is God's judgment on a world filled with violence, and the chapter does not soften it: every living thing on land dies. The judgment is thorough because the corruption was thorough. Scripture later uses the flood as a pattern for final judgment, a warning that God does not overlook evil forever.

Inside the judgment is a rescue. God himself brings Noah into the ark, preserves the animals, and shuts the door. The pattern of salvation through judgment, not around it, begins here and runs through the Passover, the Red Sea, and the cross.

The chapter shows that the ordered world of Genesis 1 depends on God's continuing will. The waters above and below that he separated come back together at his word. Creation is not self-sustaining; its boundaries hold because God holds them.

words.note: Tehom, the deep. It is the same word used in 1:2, where darkness was over the surface of the deep before God began to order the world. In poetry it can stand for the primeval ocean or the depths of the sea. Its return in 7:11 signals that the flood is a return toward the formless state before creation.

Arubbah, window or opening, translated floodgates. It is used for windows in houses and for openings in a dovecote, and in the phrase windows of heaven for sudden abundance from above (2 Kings 7:2; Malachi 3:10). Here those windows pour out judgment rather than blessing.

Gavar, to prevail or be strong, used four times in verses 18 to 24 for the waters. It is often used of armies or of one person overpowering another. The waters are pictured almost as a conquering force, overwhelming everything but the ark.

Sagar, to shut or close. Then the LORD shut him in. The verb is simple, but the subject is surprising. Noah built the ark and went inside, yet God closes the door. It is a sign of God's personal protection, and it also means the time for entering is over.

christ: Jesus refers to this very moment when he warns that people were eating, drinking, and marrying “up to the day Noah entered the ark” (Matthew 24:38), and then the flood came. His point is that his coming will arrive with the same suddenness, finding people unprepared. Peter sees in the flood a pattern of judgment and salvation. He writes that God waited patiently while the ark was being built and that eight people “were saved through water” (1 Peter 3:20), and he connects this with baptism, which saves through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. In 2 Peter 3:5-7 he sets the flood beside the final judgment, saying “the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire” and that the same word of God that brought the flood will bring that day. These readings treat the flood as a real act of God that shows the shape of his final work, judging evil and bringing his people through it. They are the New Testament's own connections, not hidden meanings found in the details of Genesis 7.

hard.q: Did the flood cover the whole planet, or was it a regional flood?
hard.a:
Christians who share the same confession about God's judgment and mercy read the flood in several ways. The global view takes the language of verse 19, all the high mountains under all the heavens, at face value and holds that the whole earth was covered. Many who hold it also argue that the flood explains much of the earth's geology, a view popularized by John Whitcomb and Henry Morris in The Genesis Flood (1961). The local or regional view notes that the Hebrew word for earth also means land, and that universal language elsewhere in Genesis clearly has a limited scope, as when every nation came to Egypt to buy grain (41:57). On this reading the flood covered the whole world known to Noah, perhaps in Mesopotamia, and destroyed the humanity of that region. A third group sees a real flood memory behind the text, told in the universal terms of ancient storytelling to make a theological point about the whole human race.

The global view appeals to the text's emphatic language and to the New Testament's comparison of the flood with the final judgment. The regional view appeals to geology, to the use of Hebrew words, and to the difficulty of fitting every animal kind into the ark. What all these readers affirm is what the chapter teaches plainly: God judges human evil, he remembers his own, and he preserves life through judgment.

questions: Noah had to enter the ark before there was any sign of rain, trusting only God's word. Where are you being asked to act on God's word before you can see why?
The LORD shut Noah in. How does it change the picture of Noah's safety to know that it was God, not Noah, who closed the door?
The flood reverses creation, returning the world toward chaos. Where do you see the effects of human sin undoing the good order of the world or of people's lives?
